opus-5.5.text:
There were quite a few, but a couple really stand out.

The first was the very early days, when the compiler first ran end to end. Before Taichi, writing a high-performance physics simulator meant hand-tuning CUDA, juggling memory layouts, and writing thousands of lines of fairly painful code. I had this idea that you could separate *what* you want to compute from *how* the data is laid out and how it's parallelized, and let a compiler handle the hard part. When I finally wrote a simulation in a few dozen lines of Taichi and it ran as fast as, sometimes faster than, my hand-written version, that was a real "wow, this actually works" moment. Until then it was just a hypothesis in my head.

The second was when we made Taichi differentiable, the DiffTaichi work. Seeing gradients flow back through an entire physical simulation, and then watching a little soft-body robot learn to walk because the optimizer could see how its actions affected the physics, was magical. It felt like we'd connected two worlds, physical simulation and machine learning, that hadn't talked to each other very easily before.

The third wasn't technical at all. It was when the community started to grow. People I'd never met began using Taichi for things I'd never imagined, like art, teaching, and research in fields far from graphics. Students would send me beautiful little demos, and people contributed backends and features. When something you built starts to have a life of its own beyond you, that's probably the most rewarding feeling of all.

r001.rationale: Describes high-performance physics simulation as painful in CUDA, then says a few dozen lines of Taichi matched or beat the hand-written version—an exciting discovery that Taichi was easier to use in that niche.

r002.rationale: The response mentions differentiable Taichi and a soft-body robot, but not the Chain Queen simulator or making it differentiable with two lines of code.

r003.rationale: It says a compiler handled hard implementation details and separately describes making Taichi differentiable, but does not state that easy differentiation required Hu to have built the compiler himself.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. There were a few moments that really stood out.

The first was the very beginning, back around 2016 when I was a PhD student at MIT. I was writing physics simulations by hand in C++ and CUDA, and every time I wanted to try a new idea, it meant days of rewriting low-level code. At some point I realized the real bottleneck wasn't the math, it was the programming. So I asked myself: what if you could write a simulation in something that looked like Python, and have it run as fast as hand-tuned CUDA? Deciding to actually build that compiler, instead of just complaining about the problem, was exciting and honestly a little scary.

The second moment was the first time the whole pipeline worked end to end. I wrote a small particle simulation, maybe a few dozen lines, hit run, and it compiled through the Taichi backend and ran on the GPU at a speed that would have taken me a week to achieve manually. Seeing those particles move on screen, from code that short, was the moment I knew the idea was real.

Then there was the 99-line MLS-MPM demo. I wanted to show that a full material point method simulation, with snow, jelly, and water interacting, could fit on a single screen. When that went around the internet and people started sending me their own variations, it was the first time I felt Taichi had left my laptop and become something other people cared about.

And the last one was open-sourcing it and watching the community grow. Getting a pull request from someone I had never met, who had read the compiler code and improved it, was a different kind of excitement. It stopped being my project and became a shared one. That shift, from a research tool to something used in graphics, robotics, and even education, is probably what I am proudest of.

r001.rationale: The response describes wanting Python-like simulation code with CUDA-level speed, but does not say Hu discovered Taichi was easier to use than CUDA within a particular niche.

r002.rationale: It does not mention automatic differentiation, the Chain Queen simulator, or making that simulator differentiable in two lines of code.

r003.rationale: It says Hu chose to build a compiler to address programming friction, but does not connect building the compiler to making the simulator differentiable easily.

astra-6.text:
One of the most exciting moments was seeing a small amount of Taichi code turn into a simulation that was both visually interesting and fast. You write down a few physical rules, run the program, and suddenly something comes alive on the screen. That connection between mathematics, programming, and graphics is really satisfying to me.

Another exciting part was seeing other people use Taichi. When you build a programming language, you have certain examples in mind. Then someone comes along with a problem you hadn’t thought about and makes something wonderful. That’s when it starts to feel bigger than your own project. You’re giving people a tool to explore their ideas, and they’re showing you what the tool can become.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses Taichi code producing fast, visually interesting simulations, but does not mention that Taichi was easier to use than CUDA in a particular niche.

r002.rationale: It does not mention automatic differentiation, the Chain Queen simulator, or making it differentiable with two lines of code.

r003.rationale: It says nothing about building a compiler oneself being necessary to make the simulator differentiable so easily.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the most exciting moments were when an idea turned into something you could actually see running. With a programming language, you spend a lot of time working on things that are invisible—the compiler, the abstractions, the details of execution. Then you run a simulation, and suddenly all that work produces motion on the screen. That’s very satisfying.

And there’s another kind of excitement when someone else uses what you’ve built. They take the language and do something you hadn’t imagined. That’s when it starts to feel bigger than your own project.
